cues.text: A Teacher in Calcutta
Born Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu in 1910 in Skopje, in what is now North Macedonia, to a devout Albanian family, she left home at eighteen to join the Sisters of Loreto , an Irish missionary order.
She took the name Teresa after St. Thérèse of Lisieux .
Sent to India, she taught for nearly two decades at a Loreto convent school in Calcutta, rising to become the school's principal.
'A Call Within a Call'
On September 10, 1946, while traveling by train to a retreat in Darjeeling, Teresa experienced what she later described as a second, more urgent call.
It was an inspiration to leave the security of convent teaching and go directly to serve the poorest people living in Calcutta's slums.
It took nearly two years of testing and discernment before her superiors granted permission for her to act on it.
Beginning Among the Poorest

After brief medical training, Teresa began her new ministry on December 21, 1948, entering the slums to visit the sick, wash the wounds of neglected children, and care for the dying with her own hands.
In a society where poverty was sometimes viewed through the lens of karma, this represented a genuinely radical act of solidarity.
Former students soon joined her, and by 1950 the community numbered twelve.
The Missionaries of Charity

On October 7, 1950, the Holy See formally approved Teresa's new religious community, the Missionaries of Charity , dedicated specifically to serving 'the poorest of the poor' — those whom, in Teresa's words, 'nobody was prepared to look after.'

The congregation expanded rapidly, opening hospices for the dying, homes for abandoned children, and eventually houses across nearly every continent, including within many communist countries during the Cold War.
Global Recognition
Teresa's work brought her international acclaim, including the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize.
She accepted it, characteristically, 'in the name of the hungry, of the naked, of the homeless...
people who have become a burden to the society, and are ashamed by everybody.'

She remained personally engaged in the direct, hands-on care of the poor even as she became one of the most recognized religious figures of the twentieth century, sought out by world leaders wherever she traveled.
Legacy
Teresa stepped down as head of the Missionaries of Charity in March 1997 due to declining health and died in Calcutta that September, honored with a state funeral by the Indian government.
Canonized in 2016 by Pope Francis, she remains one of the most universally recognized saints of the modern era.

The Missionaries of Charity she founded continue operating in some of the poorest and most difficult settings across the globe, still guided by her insistence on seeing Christ in 'the distressing disguise of the poor.'
